frames.narration: Three replicas of a post's like counter and tag set start in sync: 10 likes (slots A=4, B=3, C=3) and the tag set {urgent}, added once by A under the unique tag A0.
A network partition cuts the three replicas off from each other. Each keeps accepting writes locally, with no coordination and no waiting.
Concurrent writes. A: 3 likes, and removes urgent. B: 5 likes, and adds urgent again under a new tag B0. C: 3 likes, 1 unlike, and adds billing. Nobody can see anybody else's change.
The partition heals. Replicas send each other their whole state. A naive last-write-wins counter would now keep only C's 12, the newest write, and throw away 8 of the 10 net increments.
Each replica merges what it received: element-wise max per slot, union of tags, union of tombstones. After one round nobody has everything yet, and that is fine.

A second round of the same exchange finishes the job. All three hold P[7,8,6] N[0,0,1] = 20, which is exactly 10 + 3 + 5 + 3 - 1, and the set {billing, urgent}: B's re-add used a tag A had never seen, so A's remove could not kill it (add wins).
A delayed duplicate of A's old state arrives at C. Merging it changes nothing, because merge is idempotent and monotone. Order and repetition do not matter, so no exactly-once delivery is needed.

The limit: merge cannot enforce an invariant. If each replica accepts 8 unlikes because it sees 10 locally, the merged value is 10 - 24 = -14. A floor at zero or a unique username needs coordination, which is exactly what CRDTs avoid.
